module.tls_certificate.checks: Checks the certificate served over HTTPS: validity, chain of trust, covered name, expiry date and negotiated TLS protocol version.
module.tls_certificate.fix:
Find where HTTPS is handled: web server, load balancer, CDN or host. The certificate and the TLS settings are changed there, not on the application behind it.
If HTTPS is unavailable: open port 443 (firewall, security group or host rule), enable TLS listening on the server, install a certificate on it, then redirect HTTP to HTTPS.
If the certificate is invalid (expired, self-signed, name mismatch, unknown authority, incomplete chain): get one from a recognised authority (Let's Encrypt is free) that covers exactly the site's names, for example `example.com` and `www.example.com`.
Install the full-chain file (site certificate followed by the intermediate certificates: `fullchain.pem` with Certbot) and the matching private key, then reload the server.
If the certificate expires in less than 30 days: renew it now. Then automate renewal (Certbot, acme.sh, Caddy which does it by itself, or the host's tool) and test it with `certbot renew --dry-run`.
If an obsolete protocol is negotiated (SSLv3, TLS 1.0 or TLS 1.1): allow only TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3 in the server configuration (see the snippet). The "Deep TLS" module details the cipher suites.
Check: `openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com` must end with "Verify return code: 0 (ok)" and show the right certificate. Then run the scan again.
module.tls_certificate.title: TLS certificate
module.tls_certificate.why: An invalid or expired certificate triggers warnings for visitors or trains them to ignore warnings; an old protocol allows traffic interception.
